definition: A strong desire to do or achieve something.
examples_general: My ambition is to one day become Prime Minister. | He has no ambition in life. | Annette is a very ambitious businesswoman. | Mr Smith’s ambition to be the richest man in the world made him money-obsessed and greedy. | You should be ambitious for your future. | My ambition led to my downfall because I tried to achieve too much too soon.
examples_draft: Macbeth’s ambition to become king drives him to murder Duncan. | Lady Macbeth’s ambition is just as strong as her husband’s. | Walton’s ambition makes him say “one man’s life or death were but a small price to pay for the knowledge which I sought”.
synonyms: Drive; desire; aim; determination; Drive; determination; confidence; entitlement
notes: Frankenstein lesson wording of the definition: Wanting to achieve great things in your life.

definition: A character flaw that leads to their downfall in a tragedy.
examples_text: Shakespeare presents Macbeth’s hamartia as his over-ambitious nature. | If it was not for his hamartia, Macbeth would not have had a downfall.
notes: Also called a fatal flaw.

definition: Make secret plans with someone to commit a harmful act.
examples_text: Witches are conspiring to destroy the natural order. | In Jacobean times, people feared that witches might conspire against the King.

definition: Someone who uses underhand tactics to harm, trick or lead others astray.
examples_text: Witches are devious creatures. | Witches use devious methods to corrupt innocent people.

definition: When someone or something seems to represent what it means to be “manly”.
examples_text: When the Captain describes Macbeth, he seems to be an embodiment of masculinity. | Macbeth is an embodiment of masculinity because he is a brave and fearless fighter in battle.
synonyms: Symbol of how to be a “man”

definition: A character who begins the play in a position of high status in society and is deeply respected by others, but who has a hamartia (fatal flaw) that leads to their downfall.
notes: Defined in the lesson text, not on a Key Vocabulary slide.

definition: A Scottish lord.
notes: Defined in brackets in the lesson, not on a Key Vocabulary slide.

definition: An unavoidable future that you cannot control.
examples_text: After the prophecy, Macbeth’s fate was sealed.
examples_general: A person cannot change their fate once it has been decided.

definition: The power to choose your own path without influence.
examples_general: Some people believe that their lives are not controlled by fate but they have free will. | He chose to commit a crime so it was of his own free will.
examples_draft: Macbeth acts of his own free will when he chooses to murder Duncan. | The witches predict the future, but they never force Macbeth to use his free will for evil.

definition: Something that is unavoidable.
examples_general: Death is inevitable for all of us. | Daniel’s fate was inevitable and there was nothing he could do to stop it.
examples_draft: After the witches’ prophecy, Macbeth’s downfall seems inevitable. | As a tragic hero, Macbeth’s fall is inevitable because of his hamartia.

definition: A prediction of what will happen in the future.
notes: Defined on the lesson starter slide, not on a Key Vocabulary slide.

definition: Something that prompts and encourages the events to happen.
examples_text: The witches are a catalyst for Macbeth’s downfall. | Macbeth’s ambition is a catalyst for his downfall because it encourages him to commit evil acts of violence.

definition: Going against what you expect of how men or women should behave.
examples_text: The witches are presented as women, but Shakespeare subverts gender expectations because they have beards too. | Women in Jacobean times were expected to be submissive and gentle, so women who were dominant and strong subverted the expectations of gender.
synonyms: Defy gender expectations; challenge gender expectations

definition: Lying or tricking someone.
examples_text: Macbeth’s deception is when he hides his violent ambition from the characters around him. | Banquo does not trust the witches and he believes they are being deceptive.

definition: Giving a false outward appearance.
examples_general: Donald Trump said he was not sad he lost the election but this was a façade. | Sophie was extremely scared but had a façade of confidence. | The serial killer hid his crimes behind a façade of kindness.
examples_draft: Lady Macbeth tells her husband to put on a façade of friendliness when Duncan arrives at the castle. | Macbeth keeps up a façade of grief after the murder, even though he killed Duncan.
notes: Also taught in Jekyll and Hyde lessons 15 and 16 with the same definition. Inspector Calls lesson 2 adds the example: The serial killer hid his crimes behind a façade of kindness.
texts: Macbeth; Jekyll and Hyde; An Inspector Calls
topic: Deception; Sin; Façades; Set and Stage Directions
lesson: Macbeth lesson 7; Jekyll and Hyde lesson 15; Inspector Calls lesson 2

definition: The belief that God has chosen and anointed the King to rule.
examples_text: Many Jacobeans believed in the Divine Right to Rule, the belief that the King was chosen by God. This meant an act against the king was an act against God.
notes: Divine means Godly or ‘of God’.

definition: The belief that a host should guard and protect their guests from harm.
examples_text: Medieval society believed in the Duties of Hospitality, the belief that a host should guard and protect their guests. This meant if a host betrayed their duties, they were committing a terrible sin.
notes: Hospitality means the act of hosting guests and visitors.

definition: A speech where the character expresses their inner thoughts and feelings to the audience.
notes: Defined in the lesson text, not on a Key Vocabulary slide.

definition: A relative.
notes: Defined in the lesson text (soliloquy answers), not on a Key Vocabulary slide.

definition: Make a man feel like they are not “manly” enough.
examples_text: Lady Macbeth emasculates her husband when she commands him to do what she tells him. | It is ironic that Macbeth feels emasculated by his wife because others view him as an embodiment of masculinity.
notes: Means threatening a person’s masculinity by suggesting they are too weak and womanly.

definition: Make someone feel small and worthless.
examples_text: Lady Macbeth belittles her husband by suggesting he is weak and unable to commit the murder like he promised. | It is ironic that Macbeth feels belittled because he is a powerful and respected thane who others admire and look up to.
notes: Means putting someone down and making them feel less important.

definition: Seeing something that is not real but is created by the mind.
examples_general: When I was dehydrated, I had a hallucination of a glass of water. | The artist and poet, William Blake, described how he had hallucinations of angels visiting him.
examples_draft: The floating dagger could be a hallucination created by Macbeth’s guilty mind. | Banquo’s ghost may be a hallucination because only Macbeth can see it.

definition: Using magic to make something appear in physical form.
examples_text: The witches conjured an evil spirit to haunt the poor girl and her family.
examples_general: As if by conjuration, I suddenly found the hat I had been searching for.

definition: Feeling overwhelmed by an emotion, like it is swallowing you.
examples_text: In the poem ‘Bayonet Charge’, the soldier is consumed by his fear and trauma.
examples_general: When my father died, I was consumed by grief and sadness. | Shanice was consumed by the desire for revenge and would never stop until she achieved it. | Alexis was consumed by fear as she prepared for her sky-dive.
examples_draft: Macbeth is consumed by guilt after he murders Duncan. | Lady Macbeth is consumed by guilt and begins to sleepwalk.
notes: Lesson 24 review quiz also defines it as: being swallowed by an emotion. Remains lesson (word: consume): being eaten or swallowed by a feeling or emotion (synonyms: overwhelmed, plagued). Example: Alexis was consumed by fear as she prepared for her sky-dive. Easter sheet: overwhelmed by emotion.
lesson: Macbeth lesson 11; Power and Conflict: Remains

definition: Trying to stop or hide an emotion by burying it deep down.
examples_general: You should try to suppress your anger before it gets out of control. | For years, the girl was so shy that she suppressed her desire to put up her hand in class.
examples_draft: Lady Macbeth tries to suppress her guilt by saying “A little water clears us of this deed”. | In Act 5, Macbeth tries to suppress his fear by telling himself he bears a charmed life.
notes: Lesson 24 review quiz also defines it as: hiding or burying an emotion deep down.

definition: The way things should naturally be in the universe.
examples_text: When Duncan is king, the natural order is maintained. | By murdering Duncan, Macbeth breaks the natural order.

definition: Something that is magical and unnatural.
notes: Also defined in lesson 24 as: describes something unnatural that cannot be explained by science. Defined on the lesson starter slide, not on a Key Vocabulary slide.

definition: Feeling like people are trying to get you, making you scared and suspicious.
examples_general: Agatha was paranoid when she walked home, so would constantly look over her shoulder to see if she was followed. | Tyler was paranoid that people would steal his answers, so he always covered his work.
examples_draft: Macbeth becomes paranoid that Banquo will betray him. | Paranoid about losing the crown, Macbeth sends murderers to kill Banquo and Fleance.

definition: This establishes the tragic hero and their hamartia.
notes: Freytag’s five act structure: Act 1. Defined in the lesson, not on a Key Vocabulary slide.

definition: Here the situation worsens because of the early decisions of the tragic hero.
notes: Freytag’s five act structure: Act 2. Defined in the lesson, not on a Key Vocabulary slide.

definition: This is the turning point where the tragic hero’s plans go wrong.
examples_text: A pivotal moment is when Victor creates the monster. Before, he was full of excitement and ambition, but after he was horrified. | A pivotal moment is when William is murdered because Victor realises there are terrible consequences for his actions.
notes: Freytag’s five act structure: Act 3. Defined in the lesson, not on a Key Vocabulary slide. Frankenstein lesson wording of the definition: An important moment that changes something in the story.

definition: This shows the gradual downfall of the tragic hero.
notes: Freytag’s five act structure: Act 4. Defined in the lesson, not on a Key Vocabulary slide.

definition: Here the tragic hero finally suffers their tragic fate, usually death.
examples_draft: Sheila and Eric want a resolution in which the family accepts responsibility, but their parents refuse. | Priestley does not give the audience a neat resolution at the end of the play.
notes: Freytag’s five act structure: Act 5. Defined in the lesson, not on a Key Vocabulary slide. Inspector Calls lesson 17 defines it as: when the story ends with the problems being resolved (synonym: a happy ending). Examples: The writer created a resolution for the characters at the end of the story. | I really hope that there is a resolution at the end because I like happy endings.

definition: Giving something a physical form or body.
examples_general: Jesus is an embodiment of God’s teachings and wisdom. | My new-born baby is the embodiment of all my hopes for a happy family.
examples_draft: Banquo’s ghost is the embodiment of Macbeth’s guilt. | Lady Macbeth wants to become the embodiment of cruelty when she asks the spirits to “unsex” her. | William is an embodiment of innocence and purity. | The De Lacey family are an embodiment of a kind and loving family.
notes: The slide is headed Key Word. Also taught in Jekyll and Hyde lessons 1 and 7. Frankenstein lessons 8, 11 and 14 use it (“William is an embodiment of innocence and purity”).
topic: Banquo’s Ghost; Mr Utterson; The True Monster
lesson: Macbeth lesson 17; Jekyll and Hyde lesson 1; Frankenstein lesson 11

definition: This is when you know a prediction of the future, and by knowing it, you cause it to happen.
examples_general: Jared was told he would fail his exams in Year 11. This became a self-fulfilling prophecy because he became very worried and anxious about failing, so on the day of the exam he panicked and froze.
examples_draft: Some people argue that the witches’ prophecy is a self-fulfilling prophecy because Macbeth murders Duncan to make it come true. | If Macbeth had not believed the prophecy, he might never have killed Duncan, so it could be a self-fulfilling prophecy.
notes: Prophecy means prediction of the future. Self-fulfilling means it causes itself to come true.

definition: A cruel ruler who has too much power.
examples_general: The ruler was considered a tyrant because he would execute anyone who disobeyed him. | The King was a tyrant because he let his people starve.
examples_draft: By the end of the play, Macbeth is a tyrant who orders the murder of Macduff’s family. | Malcolm calls Macbeth a “tyrant” because he rules through violence and fear.
notes: Etymology: comes from the Ancient Greek term turannos. Easter sheet: a cruel ruler.
lesson: Macbeth lesson 20; Power and Conflict: Easter revision sheet

definition: The belief that a country is like a physical body, with the King being the head of the body.
examples_text: In Jacobean times, some believed in the body politic, meaning they thought that if the King was a tyrant, the whole country would suffer.
notes: Following this belief, the country suffers as one collective.

definition: This is when your mind begins to “unravel” and fall apart.
examples_text: The character in ‘Poppies’ experiences a psychological unravelling when her son is killed in conflict. | The murder of Duncan caused a psychological unravelling of Macbeth.

definition: Feeling overconfident.
examples_general: James’ hubris caused him to not revise for his exams. | Donald Trump believed he should be pope because of his strong sense of hubris. | A person’s hubris can make them think they are indestructible. | The king’s hubris led him to firing all of his advisors.
examples_draft: Macbeth’s hubris grows when he believes that no man “of woman born” can harm him. | His hubris in Act 5 makes him ignore the danger of Macduff.
notes: Jekyll and Hyde lesson 8 defines it as: the quality of being over-confident and arrogant. Ozymandias lesson defines it as: too much pride, confidence and arrogance. Easter sheet: excessive pride.
texts: Macbeth; Jekyll and Hyde; Power and Conflict
lesson: Macbeth lesson 22; Jekyll and Hyde lesson 8; Power and Conflict: Ozymandias

definition: No longer feeling shock, after experiencing something shocking or upsetting many times.
examples_general: The soldier had seen so many of his friends killed in battle, he became desensitised to death. | I was desensitised to violence after playing lots of violent video games.
examples_draft: By Act 5, Macbeth is desensitised to fear and says he has “almost forgot the taste of fears”. | Macbeth becomes desensitised to violence as he orders more and more murders.
notes: The slide says “similar words”.

definition: Describes a person who believes that life has no meaning or purpose.
examples_general: The teenager felt nihilistic because he felt that nothing had meaning anymore. | The nihilistic soldier had given up on fighting, felt the war was meaningless and stopped believing in God.
examples_draft: Macbeth sounds nihilistic when he describes life as “signifying nothing”. | After Lady Macbeth’s death, Macbeth feels nihilistic and believes that life has no meaning.
notes: Etymology: nihil is Latin for “nothing”.

definition: When a tragic hero realises something shocking, usually when it is too late to change his fate.
examples_general: In the story of Oedipus Rex, he experiences anagnorisis when he realises the man he killed was his own father. | In Star Wars, Luke Skywalker experiences anagnorisis when he realises that Darth Vader, his enemy, is his father.
examples_draft: Macbeth experiences anagnorisis when he learns that Macduff was “untimely ripped” from his mother’s womb. | His anagnorisis comes too late to change his fate.
synonyms: Moment of realisation; realising the terrible truth; epiphany
notes: The slide is headed Key Word. Jekyll and Hyde lesson 18 defines it as: when a character realises something shocking, such as realising the true identity of another character. Inspector Calls lesson 8 defines it as: when a character realises something shocking or profound.
texts: Macbeth; Jekyll and Hyde; An Inspector Calls
lesson: Macbeth lesson 24; Jekyll and Hyde lesson 18; Inspector Calls lesson 8

definition: The belief that life has no meaning or purpose.
notes: Noun form of nihilistic. Defined in the lesson review quiz, not on a Key Vocabulary slide.

definition: A society ruled and controlled by men.
notes: Defined in the lesson review quiz, not on a Key Vocabulary slide. My Last Duchess lesson: controlled by men. Easter sheet: male-dominated society. The Bayonet Charge lesson also lists patriarchy: a society run by men for men.
lesson: Macbeth lesson 24; Power and Conflict: My Last Duchess

definition: The story is told in third person (he/she), but the narrator tells it from the point of view of a character.
examples_text: Stevenson writes in third-person limited and the reader sees the events through Mr Utterson’s eyes.
examples_general: ‘The Boy in the Striped Pyjamas’ is told through a third-person limited point of view, because the reader only knows what the character Bruno knows.
notes: In other words: although the story is told in third person, the reader still sees everything through the eyes of the character.

definition: The voice that tells the story. It refers to who is telling the events, how much they know, and how the story is presented to the reader.
examples_text: Stevenson uses a third-person narrator to tell the story.
examples_general: Curious Incident is narrated in the first person by Christopher. | The narrator presents events in a factual way, making them seem believable.
notes: Narration controls what information is revealed or hidden, the order events are told in, and the tone of the story (e.g. objective, mysterious, personal).

definition: The technique by which a narrative presents information through a specific focal character or viewpoint.
examples_text: Because events are focalised through Utterson, the reader discovers the truth slowly, building suspense.
examples_general: By changing focalisation, the writer shifts the reader’s sympathy. | The limited focalisation increases tension because information is hidden from the reader.
notes: In other words: the character from whose perspective you see the story. This is different from what the writer focuses on.

definition: Getting enjoyment from watching someone else do something.
examples_general: She takes vicarious pleasure in watching her friend achieve something she once dreamed of. | Andrew had never made it into the NBA. But he got vicarious pleasure from watching his son make his way up the leagues. | Viewers gain vicarious pleasure from the luxury shown on screen, despite not living that lifestyle themselves.
examples_draft: Utterson gets vicarious pleasure from watching his friends give in to temptation, because he refuses to do so himself. | The reader gets vicarious pleasure from the mystery as Utterson hunts for Hyde.
notes: Breaking it down: vicarious means you experience pleasure “via” someone else; pleasure means enjoyment.

definition: Having two opposite sides.
examples_text: Stevenson describes the duality of London. It is respectable and yet under the surface it is dangerous. | In Chapter One, Stevenson emphasises the dual nature of London.
notes: Break the word down: ‘dual’ means two.

definition: The study of a person’s facial appearance to understand their personality.
notes: Lesson 4 describes it as the belief, led by Lombroso, that criminals were physically different to non-criminals. Defined in the lessons, not on a Key Vocabulary slide.

definition: Go beyond the limits of what is morally, socially, or legally acceptable.
examples_text: Some Victorians believed that some science was transgressing the laws of nature. | Some Victorians believed that it was morally wrong for humans to transgress the laws of nature.
examples_draft: Victor transgresses the laws of nature when he creates life. | Walton wants to transgress the limits of human exploration.
notes: Etymology: trans means across, so “transgress” means going across the limits. The slide is headed Key Word. Same slide taught in Frankenstein lesson 1; used again in lessons 3 and 11.
lesson: Jekyll and Hyde lesson 5; Frankenstein lesson 1

definition: A genre that follows a rational detective solving a crime.
examples_general: Many detective novels create a sense of mystery to intrigue the reader. | Detective novels often have a highly intelligent detective who tries to catch the criminal.
examples_draft: Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde is like a detective novel because Utterson investigates who Mr Hyde really is. | Like a detective novel, the story reveals the truth slowly, through clues such as the letter and the handwriting.
notes: Famous detectives: Sherlock Holmes, Hercule Poirot, Miss Marple. The slide is headed Key Word.

definition: A genre of literature that often explores fears, the way the past haunts the present and may include the supernatural.
examples_general: Much Gothic literature has a character who is isolated and trapped. | Gothic literature often tries to explore the darkest fears that society has.
examples_draft: Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde is Gothic literature because it explores fear, the supernatural and the dark side of London. | Hyde’s sinister house and the foggy streets create the unsettling atmosphere of Gothic literature. | ‘Frankenstein’ is Gothic because it has a monster, an isolated setting, a sense of mystery and characters turned mad.
notes: Famous texts: Dracula, Frankenstein, Wuthering Heights. The slide is headed Key Word. Features listed in the starter: ghost, monster, dark and stormy weather, isolated setting, sense of mystery, characters turned mad, wild and untamed nature, character with a dark secret. Frankenstein lesson wording of the definition: Literature that focuses on intense emotions, fear and the unknown, exploring madness and death. It became popular in the late 1700s and 1800s as a reaction against science and the Enlightenment.
lesson: Jekyll and Hyde lesson 6; Frankenstein lesson 6

definition: An essential characteristic or feature.
examples_text: Stevenson suggests that all humans have an inherent evil within them.
examples_general: Firefighting is an inherently dangerous occupation. | To be a doctor, you must be inherently clever.
synonyms: Essential characteristic; integral feature; fundamental aspect

definition: Going against religious laws and beliefs.
examples_text: Saskia is a heretic because she wants to learn witchcraft.
examples_general: Charles committed heresy when he criticised God in front of the whole church.
examples_draft: Many Victorians believed that Jekyll’s experiments were heresy because they interfered with God’s creation. | A pious book ruined with “startling blasphemies” is found in Jekyll’s cabinet, an act of heresy.
notes: Versions of the word: a heretic is a person who commits heresy.

definition: Analysing handwriting to determine someone’s personality traits.
examples_general: Darnell studied graphology so he could better understand the minds of others. | Graphology is not an exact science and people should be sceptical of it.
examples_draft: Mr Guest uses graphology when he notices that Jekyll’s handwriting looks like Hyde’s. | Graphology suggests that the matching handwriting reveals a link between the minds of Jekyll and Hyde.
notes: Versions of the word: a graphologist is a person who studies graphology. The slide is headed Key Word.

definition: Describes the long-lasting shock caused by a disturbing experience.
examples_general: The soldier was traumatised by all the terrible violence he had witnessed. | The traumatic experience of seeing a car crash caused Elijah to feel traumatised. | Denzel was traumatised after he saw a car hit his pet dog. | After being mugged, Susan was deeply traumatised and it caused her to have terrible nightmares at night.
examples_draft: Dr Lanyon is traumatised after he sees Hyde transform into Jekyll. | Lanyon’s pale face and “deep-seated terror” show how traumatised he is. | Victor is traumatised by all he has seen, which is why Walton notices his “wildness, and even madness”.
notes: Variations of the word: traumatic describes something that causes a person to be traumatised. The slide is headed Key Word. Feeling traumatised can cause people to feel anxious, struggle to sleep and feel haunted by the memory. Frankenstein lesson wording of the definition: This means feeling the long-lasting damage of a shocking and upsetting experience.
lesson: Jekyll and Hyde lesson 14; Frankenstein lesson 3

definition: Wrath, lust, greed, gluttony, pride, envy and sloth.
notes: Many Christians believe all sinful behaviour is caused by one or more of them. Listed in the lesson, not on a Key Vocabulary slide.

definition: The opposite of a sin.
notes: Defined in the lesson, not on a Key Vocabulary slide.

definition: A concept describing what is repulsive, degraded, or expelled to maintain personal identity or social rules. It provokes disgust and fascination.
examples_text: Hyde embodies the abject: his appearance and actions blur the lines between man and beast, morality and depravity.
examples_general: The abject is what we find disgusting or disturbing, but can’t completely ignore. | In horror films, blood and decay often represent the abject. | Sin separates the abject from the permissible.
notes: Etymology: from Latin abicere, “to cast away” (ab- = away, jacere = to throw). The abject is literally what has been thrown off or rejected, physically, morally or psychologically.

definition: Describes something evil, like the Devil (Satan).
examples_text: Victorian society was strictly Christian and therefore would have feared satanic practices.
examples_general: Eric is satanic because he worships the Devil and commits terrible sins.
notes: The slide is headed Key Word and lists these as similar words.

definition: When a writer describes something in a way that makes it seem like Hell.
examples_general: The writer uses hellish imagery to convey how evil and dark the setting seems. | The hellish imagery gives the impression that the characters are trapped in an eternal suffering.
examples_draft: Stevenson uses hellish imagery when he describes Jekyll’s cabinet, with its “red baize door”. | The hellish imagery of the barred windows makes the cabinet seem like a prison of suffering.
notes: Versions of the word: satanic imagery, evil imagery. The slide is headed Key Word.

definition: Something religious.
notes: Glossary on the lesson slide (“pious work” is likely a Bible). Not on a Key Vocabulary slide.

definition: Saying something disrespectful about God.
notes: Glossary on the lesson slide. Not on a Key Vocabulary slide.

definition: A story that is written in the style of diaries, letters or newspaper articles.
examples_general: I read an epistolary novel that was written as a collection of diary entries. | “Curious Incident” has sections that are epistolary because the writer includes letters from Christopher’s mother.
examples_draft: Chapter 9 of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde is epistolary because it is Dr Lanyon’s letter. | The epistolary ending splits the narrative into letters, just as Jekyll splits himself in two.
notes: Examples of epistolary novels: Curious Incident, Dracula, Frankenstein. The slide is headed Key Word.

definition: Being physically and mentally dependent on something.
examples_general: The man had an addiction to cigarettes that meant he felt it was impossible to quit smoking. | Jonah was addicted to playing video games.
examples_draft: Jekyll’s addiction to becoming Hyde grows until he can no longer control it. | Jekyll says that his “new power tempted me until I fell into slavery”, which shows how addiction takes over.

definition: Reverting to a more primitive or animalistic state.
notes: From the Easter revision sheet (Jekyll and Hyde list).
lesson: Jekyll and Hyde: Easter revision sheet

definition: Understanding the difference between right and wrong behaviour.
examples_general: The murderer had no sense of morality. | The parent taught his child a strong sense of morality as he raised him.
examples_draft: Mr Birling shows little morality when he sacks Eva Smith for asking for higher pay. | The Inspector tries to teach the Birlings a stronger sense of morality.

definition: The stage scenery and props used to create a scene.
examples_draft: The set is a comfortable dining room full of expensive furniture, which suggests the Birlings’ wealth. | The set includes a small table with a telephone, which is used in the ending.
notes: The slide is headed Key Words.

definition: The descriptions in the play explaining what happens on stage. This includes the lighting, set changes and costumes.
examples_draft: The stage directions say the lighting changes from “pink and intimate” to “brighter and harder” when the Inspector arrives. | Stage directions such as “cutting in, massively” show how the Inspector takes control.
notes: The lesson says stage directions can be used as quotes in essays. The slide is headed Key Words.

definition: When you see things in a happy and romantic way that is not the truth.
notes: Defined on a reading slide, not on a Key Vocabulary slide.

definition: When the audience knows something that the characters do not.
examples_draft: Mr Birling’s claim that the Titanic is “unsinkable” is dramatic irony, because the 1945 audience knows that it sank. | Birling’s confidence that there will be no war creates dramatic irony for an audience who had lived through two world wars.
notes: The slide is headed Key Words.

definition: Lacking knowledge or awareness.
examples_draft: Mr Birling is ignorant of the future when he says the Titanic is unsinkable. | The Birlings are ignorant of how their actions affected Eva Smith.
notes: The slide is headed Key Words.

definition: Look at closely to assess the condition and to discover any flaws.
examples_general: The man inspected the state of his car. | The army officer came to inspect the barracks of his soldiers.
examples_draft: The Inspector inspects the Birlings’ lives closely and uncovers their secrets. | Inspector Goole inspects each character’s part in Eva Smith’s death.

definition: All powerful.
examples_text: The Inspector seems omnipotent because he has a powerful presence that intimidates the Birling family.
notes: Taught again in the Power of Nature poetry (The Prelude lesson), with the same definition and the breakdown omni = all, potent = powerful. Examples: Christians believe that God is omnipotent because he has complete power and control over the universe. | Humans are weak and insignificant compared to the omnipotent power of nature.
texts: An Inspector Calls; Power and Conflict
lesson: Inspector Calls lesson 5; Power and Conflict: The Prelude

definition: All knowing.
examples_text: The Inspector seems omniscient because he seems to know everything about the Birlings, including their deepest secrets.

definition: An economic system where people own their own property and business.
examples_general: Capitalism encourages people to be competitive to make money. | There is sometimes a divide between the rich and the poor in a capitalist society.
examples_draft: Mr Birling believes in capitalism and thinks that a man has to “look after himself and his own”. | Priestley uses Mr Birling to show the greed of capitalism.
notes: Mr Birling is a capitalist.

definition: An economic system where the rich help the poor to better the whole of society.
examples_general: Socialism encourages people to share their wealth with those less fortunate. | There is less of a divide between the rich and the poor in a socialist society.
examples_draft: The Inspector represents socialism when he says “We are members of one body”. | Priestley wrote the play because he believed in socialism.
notes: Priestley was a socialist.

definition: Using someone for your own benefit, often treating them like an object.
examples_text: Mr Birling shows how many capitalists will happily exploit their workers. | Eva Smith is the victim of exploitation.
synonyms: Use; mistreating a person by taking advantage of them

definition: A message that uses the characters to make a strongly worded criticism of society.
notes: The lesson calls An Inspector Calls a “political diatribe” with a strong didactic message. Defined on a lesson slide, not on a Key Vocabulary slide.

definition: A system where society is organised into different classes.
examples_general: A class system is separated into three main groups: upper, middle and working class. | People do not have the same privileges in a class system.
examples_draft: The class system separates the wealthy Birlings from working-class people like Eva Smith. | Mrs Birling’s snobbery shows how the class system shaped attitudes in 1912.
notes: A class system is a type of hierarchy.

definition: Being fragile and at risk of harm.
examples_draft: Eva Smith is vulnerable because she has no family to help her. | Eva is vulnerable because she depends on her job to survive.
notes: The slide is headed Key Words.

definition: Having your power taken away.
examples_draft: Eva is disempowered because Mr Birling can sack her for asking for more money. | Women in 1912 were often disempowered by a patriarchal society.
notes: The slide is headed Key Words. My Last Duchess lesson: someone who has had their power taken away. Easter sheet: stripped of power.
texts: An Inspector Calls; Power and Conflict
lesson: Inspector Calls lesson 7; Power and Conflict: My Last Duchess

definition: Those with the most power and wealth. Often these are aristocracy who have inherited land and titles.
notes: Defined on a lesson slide, not on a Key Vocabulary slide.

definition: Those with some power and wealth. They have professional jobs, often working in business, and often enjoy privileges and opportunities not available to the working class.
notes: Defined on a lesson slide, not on a Key Vocabulary slide.

definition: People with low-paying jobs, often manual work. These are often the poorest people in society.
notes: Defined on a lesson slide, not on a Key Vocabulary slide.

definition: An immoral act against God.
examples_text: Mr Birling is sinful for keeping his money all to himself.
examples_general: It was a sin when I pushed my brother in anger.
notes: Christians believe that there are seven deadly sins that are the cause of other sinful behaviour.

definition: A medieval play that taught the audience how to be good people.
notes: Characters stand for ideas, make bad choices, are given a chance to change, and the play teaches a clear lesson. Defined on a lesson slide, not on a Key Vocabulary slide.

definition: To use or take advantage of someone (verb).
examples_text: Mr Birling exploits the working class to make as much money as he can. | Priestley highlights how the exploitation of the working class is unfair and immoral.
notes: Related word: exploitation (noun).

definition: To treat someone disrespectfully and make them feel inferior.
examples_general: You should never try to degrade someone else. | I feel degraded when I am told I am worthless.
examples_draft: Mrs Birling degrades Eva by calling her “a girl of that sort”. | Mr Birling degrades his workers by treating them as “cheap labour”.
notes: The slide lists these as related words.

definition: Wants things in society to change and improve for the better.
examples_text: Priestley’s socialist views were very progressive.
examples_general: I voted for the president with the more progressive beliefs because I want society to change.
notes: Related words: progress means wants things to improve.

definition: Wants things in society to stay the same and resists change.
examples_general: Daniel had conservative views and believed that women should not work but should be housewives. | Some politicians might have conservative views because they want to maintain traditional attitudes to society.
examples_draft: Mr Birling has conservative views because he wants society to stay the way it is. | Mrs Birling’s conservative attitudes make her refuse to help Eva Smith.
notes: Related words: conserve means keep things as they are.

definition: Judging someone based upon bias without proper reasons or evidence (a thought).
examples_general: The man’s prejudice meant he assumed that women were not as intelligent as him. | Those living in poverty often experience class prejudice because it is sometimes assumed that they are lazy, uneducated and immoral.
examples_draft: Mrs Birling’s class prejudice makes her assume that Eva is lying. | The Inspector challenges the Birlings’ prejudice against the working class.
notes: Break down the word: pre-judge.

definition: Treating someone differently and unfairly due to a prejudiced view (an action).
examples_general: Many black people experience discrimination in the workplace. | Charlene felt discriminated against because she was not listened to by her male co-workers, even though she was correct. | Discriminatory behavior is unacceptable.
examples_draft: Eva Smith experiences discrimination because of her class and her gender. | Mrs Birling discriminates against Eva by refusing her help at the charity.
notes: Variations of the word: discriminatory (adjective), discriminates (verb).

definition: Using your power unfairly to mistreat or hurt others.
examples_general: The security guard abused their power when they let their friend steal from the shop. | The king abused his power when he ordered all his enemies to be executed. | A good leader does not abuse their power.
examples_draft: Mr Birling abuses his power when he sacks Eva Smith for asking for higher pay. | Sheila abuses her power when she gets Eva dismissed from Milwards because she is jealous.
synonyms: Misrule; corrupt; mistreat others with less power

definition: Taking responsibility for something and accepting that you have a duty to take care of it.
examples_general: Destiny worked as a shop manager and was accountable for making sure he locked the store every night. | Trinity refused to take accountability for not completing her homework.
examples_draft: Sheila feels accountable for getting Eva Smith dismissed from Milwards. | Mr Birling refuses to be held accountable for what happened to Eva Smith.

definition: When the story ends with things being unresolved, often finishing with a dramatic moment.
examples_general: At the end of the story, there was a cliff-hanger because it was unclear if the main character survived the fight. | I love a cliff-hanger ending because it leaves me always wanting more.
examples_draft: An Inspector Calls ends with a cliff-hanger when the telephone rings to say a girl has died and an inspector is on his way. | The final phone call is a cliff-hanger because we do not know what will happen to the Birlings.
synonyms: A shocking ending; a dramatic ending

definition: When the ending links in some way to the beginning of the story.
examples_general: The writer created a circular narrative by describing a terrible storm at both the beginning and end of the story. | A circular narrative can make the reader feel like the events will happen again.
examples_draft: The ending of An Inspector Calls feels like a circular narrative because another inspector is about to arrive, just as the first one did. | A circular narrative suggests that the Birlings may face the same questions again.

definition: Pointless and meaningless (adjective).
examples_text: Some war poets explore the futility of conflict in their poems.
examples_general: War seems futile because so many lives are lost for no reason.
examples_draft: Tennyson suggests the charge was futile because the soldiers died because of a mistake. | Owen presents the war as a futile cause in ‘Exposure’.
notes: Variations of the word: futility (abstract noun).
lesson: Power and Conflict: Charge of the Light Brigade

definition: People who are sent to their deaths by being told to charge at the enemy’s cannons.
examples_general: In WW1, many of the soldiers were treated like cannon-fodder and were sent to their deaths. | Daniel could see the enemy’s weapons and knew he was cannon-fodder.
examples_draft: In ‘The Charge of the Light Brigade’, the soldiers are treated as cannon-fodder when they ride into the valley because of a mistake. | The Light Brigade are cannon-fodder because someone had blundered.
notes: Break down the word: fodder means food, so cannon-fodder literally means being fed to the cannons.
lesson: Power and Conflict: Charge of the Light Brigade

definition: A narrative poem often spoken aloud (usually to remember famous tragedies, battles or heroes).
notes: Defined on a lesson slide, not on a Key Vocabulary slide.
lesson: Power and Conflict: Charge of the Light Brigade

definition: Discovering something is not as good as you thought.
examples_text: I always dreamed of going to USA, but I became disillusioned when I got there and experienced many rude Americans.
examples_general: I dreamed of becoming a boxer but was disillusioned when I saw the brain damage that many professional boxers suffered.
examples_draft: The soldier in ‘Bayonet Charge’ is disillusioned because the war is nothing like the propaganda promised. | In ‘Exposure’, Owen shows soldiers who are disillusioned about the glory of war.

definition: A psychological condition caused by a traumatic event. Long after the event, the person experiences intense, disturbing thoughts and emotions.
examples_general: After witnessing a car accident, I experienced PTSD when I would have panic attacks when I’d get inside a car. | Charlotte developed PTSD after being in an abusive relationship with her boyfriend.
examples_draft: The soldier in ‘Remains’ suffers from PTSD because he cannot forget the looter he shot. | Armitage suggests PTSD when the speaker says “But I blink and he bursts again”.
notes: Shell shock is what it was called during WW1.

definition: Having a misplaced belief in things that are clearly not true.
notes: Defined on a lesson slide, not on a Key Vocabulary slide.

definition: Pride and love for one’s country.
notes: Keywords slide, not a Key Vocabulary slide.

definition: Love for one’s country to an extreme (to the detriment of other nations).
notes: Keywords slide, not a Key Vocabulary slide.

definition: Something you can throw away or dispose of easily.
examples_general: In WW1, many of the soldiers were treated as disposable, as though their lives were not valuable. | The way so many men are sent to their deaths in war, suggests that those in command view them as disposable.
examples_draft: The pilot in ‘Kamikaze’ is treated as disposable by those who command him. | The soldiers in ‘The Charge of the Light Brigade’ are disposable to their commanders.

definition: Repeating a belief to someone until they accept it without question.
examples_general: In Nazi Germany, many young children were indoctrinated into believing that Germans were superior to other races. | Helena believed that her parents indoctrinated her into believing that she must be married by 25 years old.
examples_draft: The pilot in ‘Kamikaze’ has been indoctrinated with patriotic ideas, shown by the “powerful incantations”. | The soldier in ‘Bayonet Charge’ was indoctrinated by propaganda to believe that war was glorious.

definition: A turning point in a poem.
examples_text: Many poets create a volta to show the way that a character changes. | Samantha thought that the beginning of the poem was dark and depressing but after the volta it became hopeful.
examples_draft: The volta in ‘Remains’ comes at “End of story, except not really”, when the conflict moves into the soldier’s mind. | In ‘The Prelude’, the mountain appearing is a volta because the speaker’s attitude changes.
synonyms: A poem’s turning point; a poem’s pivotal moment
lesson: Power and Conflict: Comparison on Bravery and Fear

definition: Feeling like you are in the presence of a higher or greater power. It is so great and powerful it is difficult to fully understand.
examples_general: When I entered the church, I could feel the sublime presence of God. | Staring at the mountain, I felt the sublime power of nature. | The monk often experienced the sublime when he looked at the beautiful and grand ceiling of the monastery.
examples_draft: The speaker in ‘The Prelude’ experiences the sublime when the mountain towers above him. | Wordsworth shows the sublime power of nature through the “huge and mighty forms”.
notes: Context: it is often used when explaining ideas about the power of God or nature.

definition: A collection of philosophers, writers and artists in the later 18th century who had shared ideas about humanity and society: nature is supreme, people should follow their emotions and imagination, and people should not be controlled but should be free.
examples_text: Mary Shelley’s own husband, Percy Bysshe Shelley, wrote many famous works of the Romantic Movement, including ‘Ozymandias’ and ‘Prometheus Unbound’.
notes: Defined on lesson slides, not on a Key Vocabulary slide. Easter sheet word: Romanticism (the belief that nature is powerful and should be respected). Built from the lesson’s fill-in paragraphs. Key writers named: Wordsworth, Coleridge, Percy Shelley. Frankenstein lesson wording of the definition: A group of writers and artists who emerged at the end of the 18th century and continued into the 19th. They hated industrialisation and loved the natural world.
lesson: Power and Conflict: The Prelude; Frankenstein lesson 2

definition: A long narrative poem that tells the story of a hero’s journey as they embark on a grand adventure.
notes: Defined on a lesson slide, not on a Key Vocabulary slide. The Prelude is autobiographical, and its journey is a psychological one.

definition: A person who has once served in the army and has experienced conflict.
examples_general: Jared was a war veteran who had fought in many wars during his career. | Many war veterans struggle to readjust to life after the army.
examples_draft: The speaker in ‘Remains’ is a war veteran haunted by a memory. | Armitage gives a voice to war veterans in ‘Remains’.
synonyms: Ex-soldier; retired soldier with lots of experience

definition: A photographer who takes images to be used by the news to tell the news story.
examples_text: Jerica was a photojournalist who had taken many powerful images of the wars she had witnessed in her career.
examples_general: Many photojournalists put themselves in dangerous situations to capture photos for the news.
examples_draft: The speaker in ‘War Photographer’ is a photojournalist who develops his pictures in a darkroom. | The photojournalist in Duffy’s poem remembers the suffering he has witnessed.
notes: Types of photojournalist include sport news and celebrity news; the character in the poem is a war photographer.

definition: Sharing part-responsibility for wrong-doing with other people.
examples_general: Philip saw someone stealing but did not call the police. This meant he was complicit in the crime. | Mr and Mrs Todd both failed to feed their cat for a week. This meant they were complicit in neglecting their pet.
examples_draft: In ‘War Photographer’, the readers who ignore the suffering in the photographs are complicit. | The photographer may feel complicit because he earns his living from other people’s suffering.

definition: Not feeling concerned or interested in something.
examples_general: A Y11 student felt apathy towards his science GCSE and he did not revise at all. | Manuel was apathetic and did not feel motivated to apply for a new job.
examples_draft: Duffy suggests apathy when she writes that “they do not care”. | The apathy of the people reading the newspaper contrasts with the photographer’s trauma.

definition: Deep sadness caused by loss, often someone’s death.
examples_general: Alex felt a terrible grief when his mother died. | Chantelle was consumed by grief when her pet died.
examples_draft: The mother in ‘Poppies’ is consumed by grief for her son. | Weir shows her grief through the image of “spasms of paper red”.
notes: Why use it? It is better than the word sad or depressed because it links to loss.

definition: Something weak that can be easily broken and destroyed.
examples_text: The poet conveys the fragility of human life when he describes how easily the looter was killed in ‘Remains’.
examples_general: Paper is fragile because it can easily be ripped.
notes: The slide is headed Key words.

definition: All things (moments, emotions, life and objects) are temporary, fleeting and constantly changing.
notes: Defined on a lesson slide, not on a Key Vocabulary slide.

definition: Being unfairly treated or controlled by someone with more power.
examples_general: People suffer when they experience oppression at the hands of others. | Tyrants often oppress the people they rule.
examples_draft: Blake shows the oppression of ordinary people in ‘London’ through the “mind-forg’d manacles”. | Agard explores oppression through education in ‘Checking Out Me History’.
notes: Also taught in the Checking Out Me History lesson.

definition: Where a country takes control over the native people of an area.
examples_general: Britain colonised many countries including India. | The colonised people of India were treated unfairly by the colonialist rulers.
examples_draft: ‘Checking Out Me History’ is about the effects of colonisation on Caribbean identity. | Agard explores how Britain’s colonisation controlled what the speaker was taught.
notes: Colonialist: an adjective to describe someone who causes colonisation. Colonise: the verb for the act of colonisation.
lesson: Power and Conflict: Checking Out Me History

definition: Soldiers directly involved in the fighting.
notes: Used to sort the poems. Defined on a lesson slide, not on a Key Vocabulary slide.

definition: Other people affected by war who are not soldiers.
notes: Used to sort the poems (Easter sheet: “indirect effects – consequences that affect people not directly involved”). Defined on a lesson slide, not on a Key Vocabulary slide.

definition: Emotional shock caused by distressing events.
notes: From the Easter revision sheet.

notes: From the Easter revision sheet.

definition: A struggle between opposing forces.

notes: From the Easter revision sheet (see also Romantic Movement).

definition: To steal the powers of a God.
examples_text: Prometheus appropriates divine power when he steals the fire from Zeus. | In ‘Frankenstein’, Shelley suggests that appropriating divine power could lead to terrible consequences.
notes: Break-down: appropriate means steal or take; divine means Godly. Also used in lessons 3 and 11.

definition: A story within a story.
examples_text: Shelley creates a frame narrative, starting with Walton’s story and then changing to Frankenstein’s story. | The frame narrative emphasises how Walton and Frankenstein are similar.
examples_draft: The novel is a frame narrative because Victor’s story is told inside Walton’s letters, and the Creature’s story is told inside Victor’s.
notes: Lesson 11 describes it as “a story in a story in a story”.

definition: Feeling like you deserve special treatment or privileges.
examples_general: The student felt entitled to be automatically chosen for the main role in the school play without auditioning. | The celebrity was entitled and did not want to queue at the airport.
examples_draft: Victor’s parents treat him as their “plaything and their idol”, which may have made him entitled.
synonyms: Believes they deserve something; arrogant attitude

definition: Believing that you are better than others.
examples_general: The football star had an inflated sense of superiority because he’d been told he was amazing his whole life. | The arrogant supermodel had an inflated sense of superiority.
examples_draft: Victor’s sense of superiority grows because his parents treat him like a God.
notes: Break it down: thinking you’re better than or superior to others.

definition: Wanting to achieve great scientific discoveries.
examples_general: I have the scientific ambition to cure cancer. | Scientific ambition led to the creation of nuclear weapons, which could kill everyone on Earth.
examples_draft: Victor’s scientific ambition drives him to “pursue nature to her hiding places”.

definition: Having power or control without any limits.
examples_general: Mary Shelley warns her readers of the dangers of unchecked power. | The cruel dictator had unchecked power, meaning he could do anything he wanted without anyone to stop him.
examples_draft: Victor wants absolute power over life and death when he hopes “a new species would bless me as its creator”.
notes: The slide uses the wording “unchecked power” in its sentences.

definition: Pushing someone out of the role they should have.
examples_general: The rebel displaced the king and took his throne. | The Grade-A student felt displaced when others in the class started scoring higher than them.
examples_draft: By creating life, Victor tries to displace God, and also displaces women, who normally give birth.
notes: The slide is headed Key Word. Lesson 7 asks how Victor displaces God and women.

definition: Push someone to the edge of society, making them feel powerless.
examples_general: People can be cruel and will sometimes marginalise anyone who is different. | Lukas felt marginalised by society because he was a refugee and his human rights were often ignored.
examples_draft: The villagers marginalise the Creature by attacking him without trying to speak to him.

definition: Being lonely and separated from others.
examples_text: The creature experiences physical isolation because he is cut off from others inside his hovel. | The creature experiences emotional isolation because there is no one who will show him love. | The creature feels isolated.
notes: Variations: physical isolation, emotional isolation, social isolation. Lesson 14 contrasts belonging with isolation.

definition: The way a person sees themselves.
examples_text: Victor Frankenstein’s sense of self is influenced by his parents who spoil him and treat him like a God. | The deaths of William and Justine change Victor’s sense of self because he now sees himself as “the true murderer”.

definition: To treat someone like they are not human.
examples_text: Victor dehumanises the creature when he calls him a “vile insect”.
examples_draft: Victor dehumanises the Creature by calling him “demon” and “fiend” instead of seeing a person.
notes: The lesson answer is “Treat like not human”. Taught in lessons 11 and 14.

definition: The Age of Enlightenment was a period of scientific discovery and the development of knowledge from the end of the 1600s until 1815.
examples_draft: In the Age of Enlightenment, medicine and technology developed at a rapid pace, which is the world Victor grows up in.
notes: The lesson says medicine and technology developed rapidly, and explorers were discovering new parts of the world.

definition: A story that warns us of the dangers of doing something, such as transgressing the laws of nature in the hunt for divine power.
examples_draft: ‘Frankenstein’ is a cautionary tale because it warns readers about the dangers of scientific ambition.
notes: From the lesson’s challenge answer about Prometheus.

definition: The use of symbolism and strong images to allow the reader to picture what is described. It includes similes, metaphors and personification.
examples_draft: Shelley uses nightmarish imagery such as “demoniacal corpse” to describe the Creature’s birth.
notes: Also a technique: see techniques.csv.
